summary: Kickoff scoping for a 6-week POC focused on unit economics and benchmarks. Key success criteria: sub-200ms p50 for short chat queries, under $0.003 per 1k prompt tokens with batching, and no PII leaving VPC for compliance. Discussed workload mix, batching/caching knobs, staging benchmarks, and timeline. Agreed next steps and owners.
topics: success criteria; workload sizing; per-token model comparisons; batching and KV cache strategy; dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs; timeline and deliverables; security constraints (data residency/VPC)
questions: Can we hit target p50 for 256-token median requests?; What is realistic per-1k-token unit cost after batching?; How quickly can Redwood onboard a VPC connector for private test?
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-07-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Claire Mendoza (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood CSM); Maya Chen (Cascade Head of ML), Liam O'Shea (Platform Eng), Noah Grant (Finance), Priya Nair (Data Scientist)

Auto-summary: Kickoff scoping for unit economics POC focused on retail recommender/chat augmentation. Customer has tight budget runway and strict residency requirements; primary ask is a realistic cost model and bench plan.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Claire Mendoza: Okay everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we wanted to use the first 10-15 to confirm success criteria then walk into workload shape and the bench plan. Maya, want to kick off with what success looks like for Cascade?
[00:14] Maya Chen: Sure, th-thanks Claire. So for us success is three things: one, latency performance — for our short shopper chat queries we want p50 under 200ms and p95 under 600ms ideally, two, unit cost — we need to get to something like under three tenths of a cent per 1k prompt tokens after batching and caching, and three, compliance — no customer PII ever leaves our VPC during pilot. So those are the hard constraints.
[00:42] Arjun Patel: Good, that's clear. Quick clarification on that unit cost target — is that per input token only or combined prompt+generation tokens?
[00:52] Noah Grant: Finance here — when we say per-1k tokens, we're talking about billable tokens end-to-end; but for modeling we're ok to split prompts vs generations if that helps. The target is an average blended cost.
[01:08] Claire Mendoza: Great, thanks. A quick note on the VPC requirement: Redwood Private has a VPC connector option for pilot, and we can also run a dedicated pool in a customer-managed VPC. That said, spinning that up takes about 2 weeks of infra prep plus the network approvals. Is that timeline okay?
[01:28] Liam O'Shea: Two weeks is fine, but our security team will need the KMS/HSM integration details and the audit log retention plan. We can start the approvals in parallel.
[01:38] Sofia Ruiz: We'll put our security pack in the follow-up email — SOC2 scope, SSO/SAML, KMS notes.
[01:44] Priya Nair: Quick question on workload: our mix is roughly 60% short interactive chat (median 40-80 tokens), 30% mid-length Q&A (median 200-400 tokens), and 10% long-form generation for content (avg 1200 tokens) — does Redwood prefer we separate those when you run benches?
[02:05] Arjun Patel: Yes, please separate. Different seq lengths exercise different kernels; batching behavior and KV cache benefits diverge. For the short chat we can enable aggressive prefix caching and micro-batching, which is where you get the biggest per-token savings.
[02:18] Maya Chen: When you say micro-batching, what's the tradeoff on p50? I'm worried batching to save cost will push latency balloons.
[02:26] Arjun Patel: Totally. For interactive chat we typically recommend batch sizes of 1-8 with continuous batching — you get modest cost reductions with almost no p50 impact up to ~4 concurrent coalesce window. Once you push to 16 you start to see p50 creep. We'll show numbers in the bench.
[02:41] Claire Mendoza: Also we'll test prefix/KV caching. For your 60% short chats, if there are repeated product prompts we can cache completions or KV states to reduce effective tokens. Priya, do you expect a lot of repeated prompts?
[02:54] Priya Nair: Yes — product info lookups are highly repetitive, especially SKU lookups. Probably 35-40% of short chats hit the same product templates.
[03:02] Arjun Patel: That will significantly move the economics — caching can drop per-effective-token cost by 20-40% in that slice.
[03:09] Noah Grant: Okay so for pilot budget thinking, our runway allows for about $25k for infra in the next quarter. How do we budget for hosted vs dedicated?
[03:20] Claire Mendoza: Quick framing: hosted (Redwood API) gets you fastest time-to-results; unit cost there depends on model selection and batching behavior. Dedicated reserved capacity has a monthly commitment but predictable throughput and lower per-token cost at scale, plus isolation. For a 6-week pilot, we often do hosted for the benchmark and then a short dedicated eval if committed traffic looks promising.
[03:42] Liam O'Shea: We won't commit to a reserved capacity for a pilot; we just need deterministic numbers so the finance team can model worst-case runway.
[03:50] Arjun Patel: No problem. We'll run hosted benches across a few model variants — a 13B quantized variant, a 70B float & 70B quantized where available — and produce per-1k token cost assuming the batching knobs you expect. We'll also produce an estimate for dedicated pricing extrapolated to steady-state throughput.
[04:10] Maya Chen: Can you also include a variant where the model uses fused attention optimizations? We have some sequences that hit long contexts in discovery flows.
[04:19] Arjun Patel: Yes we can flag compiled kernels / fused attention; that'll show up as latency improvements on longer contexts. We'll mark which kernels were used in each bench run.
[04:27] Liam O'Shea: What's the plan for the bench workload? Synthetic vs recorded traffic?
[04:32] Arjun Patel: Prefer a hybrid. Provide us with a sampled anonymized trace (Priya to provide) and we'll augment with synthetic variations to stress the tails and long form generation. We'll run three phases: baseline single-request runs to get p50/p95, micro-batching experiments to sweep batch sizes, and caching-enabled runs.
[04:50] Priya Nair: We'll redact PII. We'll share token histograms too.
[04:54] Claire Mendoza: Timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) finalize success criteria and sample workload; week 1-2 spin up hosted benches and deliver initial cost/latency spreadsheet; week 3 run VPC connector + dedicated test if approved; week 4 deliver consolidated report and recommendations. Does that fit?
[05:13] Maya Chen: Sounds reasonable. We want the consolidated report before our board planning meeting on 2027-08-15, so earlier the better.
[05:21] Noah Grant: Also need a small appendix in the report with cost sensitivity — i.e., what happens if average prompt length rises 20% or if concurrency doubles.
[05:31] Arjun Patel: We'll include sensitivity slices.
[05:34] Claire Mendoza: Ok let's go into a quick pricing example live to anchor expectations. Arjun, can you walk through an example per-1k token math for a short chat if we use the 70B quantized model with 4x micro-batching and caching on 40% of short chats?
[05:47] Arjun Patel: Sure. High level: raw hosted inference cost per token for 70B q would be approx $0.0022 per 1k tokens without batching — approximate numbers, depends on sequence length — with micro-batching and caching that effective cost can drop to about $0.0007-$0.0012 per 1k effective tokens for the short-chat slice. Then blended across the full mix (60/30/10) you end up around $0.0016 per 1k tokens. If you enable dedicated reserved capacity extrapolated to your peak QPS we can get closer to $0.0009 per 1k tokens at steady state.
[06:22] Maya Chen: Those numbers look promising — are those inclusive of network egress and overlay infra?
[06:28] Claire Mendoza: We include compute and model runtime; network egress and additional storage (long-term logs) are separate line items and we'll list them in the spreadsheet.
[06:36] Liam O'Shea: On the VPC note — what about tokenization differences? We saw different libraries tokenize product SKUs oddly and that changed token counts.
[06:46] Arjun Patel: Good flag. Please include a few raw prompts and we'll tokenize with the same runtime we bench. We'll also surface tokenization deltas in the report.
[06:55] Priya Nair: For the bench run, can you capture p50/p90/p95 and also tail CPU on the infra side? We want to know when we hit NVlink or memory pressure.
[07:05] Arjun Patel: We'll capture GPU util, memory, and any OOM signals. For hosted runs we can give an infra-level summary, for dedicated we'll give more detailed telemetry.
[07:15] Noah Grant: Back to economics, how do model variants compare? If we pick 13B vs 70B quant, what's the relative delta in unit cost and latency?
[07:24] Arjun Patel: 13B models typically have lower latency and lower absolute compute cost but often require higher prompt engineering to hit the same quality. In rough terms the 13B q might be 30-50% lower cost and 20-40% lower latency p50, but you need to validate quality vs your tasks. We'll bring a quality comparison per task.
[07:43] Maya Chen: We'll need a small eval set of 200 examples from our core shopping flows for quality comparisons.
[07:50] Priya Nair: We'll assemble and label them this week.
[07:54] Claire Mendoza: Great. One more thing on caching: there are two knobs — prefix/KV caching and response caching. We typically recommend KV caching for chat-history-like flows and response caching for template lookups. Which is the bigger win here?
[08:08] Arjun Patel: For product SKU/template lookups response caching gives the largest win; for conversational state KV cache helps reduce autoregressive compute across long histories. For Cascade, because you have both, we'll test both and recommend default settings.
[08:20] Liam O'Shea: Any security or compliance caveats we should be aware of during bench? For example, can you guarantee that logs stored in Redwood hosted won't have PII?
[08:30] Sofia Ruiz: We can enable redaction and retention policies on hosted benches. For PII policy we'll work with your security team; for the VPC pilot we can ensure logs stay inside your project.
[08:39] Noah Grant: Ok, final commercial Q — if the pilot shows we hit your target economics, what's the typical timeline to go to production (dedicated)?
[08:48] Claire Mendoza: From signed commitment to production with dedicated capacity usually 4-8 weeks depending on approvals and infra; some large customers with strict networking need a bit longer.
[08:58] Maya Chen: That's fine.
[09:00] Claire Mendoza: Quick recap of owners and due dates then we'll wrap. Arjun will run hosted bench (1k synthetic + sampled trace) and share raw bench artifacts and a first-pass cost spreadsheet by 2027-07-26. Maya/Priya will share sample prompts and token histograms by 2027-07-22. Claire will send pilot pricing and security pack by 2027-07-23. Redwood to include a sensitivity appendix.
[09:26] Liam O'Shea: Can you also include a quick runbook for network approvals? Our infra team needs step-by-step.
[09:33] Sofia Ruiz: We'll include a networking checklist and common firewall rules.
[09:37] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Any other questions?
[09:40] Noah Grant: None.
[09:42] Claire Mendoza: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the sheet and exact bench schedule.
[09:46] Priya Nair: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript. Note: transcription contains occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "micro-batching" sometimes transcribed as "micro matching") and speaker labels may be approximate in a few places.
